entry.evidence: However, the characteristics of these reflectors have not been examined in detail, nor have they been considered in terms of fossil or active diagenetic processes

steps.action: The authors pose the question of what the cross-cutting reflectors on the Falkland/Malvinas Plateau are and whether they are active or fossil fronts, using seismic, lithological, thermal and velocity data.
steps.quote: The aim of this study is to investigate the nature of cross-cutting reflectors across the Falkland/Malvinas Plateau

steps.action: The authors take from the literature two rival origins for cross-cutting reflectors: silica diagenesis and gas-hydrate formation.
steps.quote: Cross-cutting reflectors are interpreted to be associated with secondary (post-depositional) geochemical processes, notably silica diagenesis or gas hydrate (GH) formation

steps.action: The authors take from the literature the distinct seismic predictions of each rival: positive polarity, velocity increase and no frequency drop for an Opal-A/CT front, against negative polarity with free-gas attenuation for a gas-hydrate BSR.
steps.quote: silica diagenesis results in positive amplitude reflections, whereas GHs are associated with negative amplitude reflections

steps.action: The authors adopt published geometric and structural criteria for telling an active diagenetic front from a fossilized one (BSR or NBSR, folds, polygonal faults).
steps.quote: Summary of criteria used for discerning the status of a silica diagenetic front (active vs. fossilized), modified from Varkouhi et al. (2022).

steps.action: The authors acquire and process about 3300 km of new MSM81 multichannel seismic data: semblance velocity analysis, NMO, stacking, post-stack migration, no AGC, and three attributes.
steps.quote: This study uses a subset (ca. 3300 km) of 2D seismic reflection data from the 2019 RV Maria S. Merian cruise MSM81

steps.action: The authors tie the seismic data to DSDP Sites 327, 329, 330 and 511 through core interval velocities, and extend their 2021 Maurice Ewing Bank stratigraphic model with new units SU3′ and SU6.
steps.quote: The velocity data were used to correlate information from the drill sites with seismic profiles

steps.action: The authors map reflector XR-F/MB: high amplitude, subparallel to the seafloor at 500–550 ms TWT below seafloor, same polarity as the seafloor, high energy, shoaling with water depth, locally serrated.
steps.quote: Reflector XR-F/MB has the same polarity as seafloor reflector R–SF

steps.action: The authors map reflector XR-F/MT in the trough: a continuous, high-amplitude, normal-polarity non-bottom-simulating reflector that mimics the Early-Middle Miocene unconformity R-EMM.
steps.quote: Reflector XR-F/MT is not parallel to the seafloor reflector in the F/MT; instead, it seems to replicate the geometry of reflector R-EMM

steps.action: The authors describe features next to the reflectors: layer-bound small-throw faults, anticlines and synclines above the reflectors, and higher amplitudes below XR-F/MB.
steps.quote: Numerous small-scale faults with average throws of about 40 ms TWT have deformed the strata surrounding reflector XR-F/MB

steps.action: The authors read seismic attributes across both reflectors: a semblance velocity increase of about 75 m/s, an interval-velocity increase, no change in instantaneous frequency, and little change in the first envelope derivative.
steps.quote: Across both reflectors, an average velocity increase of about 75 m/s is observed on semblance profiles.

steps.action: The authors compare the reflectors with DSDP and piston-core lithology: siliceous ooze and chert are present, as silica diagenesis requires.
steps.quote: From a lithological perspective, this supports the diagenetic nature of reflectors XR-F/MB and XR-F/MT

steps.action: The authors exclude the gas-hydrate origin because both reflectors have normal (positive) polarity, whereas a gas-hydrate BSR would be reversed; the high positive amplitudes fit an Opal-A/CT front.
steps.quote: This observation rules out their origin as GH-BSRs

steps.action: The authors check the gas-hydrate exclusion with independent attributes: there is no drop in instantaneous frequency below the reflectors and absorption is weak, so no free gas lies beneath them.
steps.quote: drop in frequency content is observed below reflectors XR-F/MB and XR-F/MT, as expected for a GH-BSR

steps.action: The authors check that the shoaling of XR-F/MB with water depth is real geometry and not a velocity artifact, by testing for lateral velocity variation.
steps.quote: no significant lateral variations in interval velocities are observed within the top 1500 ms TWT below the seafloor

steps.action: The authors interpret the layer-bound, non-oriented faults as polygonal faults and the folds as differential-compaction folds, both typical of silica transformation.
steps.quote: we categorize these as polygonal faults associated with the abrupt compaction across the TZA/CT

steps.action: The authors apply the Table 1 criteria: the NBSR geometry of XR-F/MT, and the polygonal faults and compaction folds near XR-F/MB, indicate fossilized fronts.
steps.quote: an NBSR clearly points to the presence of a fossilized diagenetic front (Table 1)

steps.action: The authors infer when the fronts were fossilized by finding the shallowest horizon with the same geometry (R-EMM in the trough, R–SF in the basin, of Middle/Late Miocene age), taken as the palaeo-seafloor.
steps.quote: The fossilization time can be estimated from identification of the shallowest horizon with the same geometry as reflector XR-F/MT

steps.action: The authors check the borehole seafloor temperatures (0.7 and 2 °C) against independent oceanographic bottom-water data, before using them as inputs.
steps.quote: These are in good agreement with oceanographic data from the F/MB

steps.action: The authors compute what an active front predicts: with an averaged gradient of 45 °C/km, a seafloor temperature of 1 °C, 550 ms TWT and 1900 m/s, the temperature at XR-F/MB would be 22.3 °C.
steps.quote: the estimated temperature at the TZA/CT equals 22.3

steps.action: The authors compare the 22.3 °C estimate with the minimum of 35 °C needed for Opal-A/CT conversion: present conditions cannot account for the front, which supports fossilization.
steps.quote: the estimated temperature at the present depth for reflector XR-F/MB lies below the minimum temperature for the onset of silica diagenesis

steps.action: The authors pose three rival mechanisms for the arrest of the front: seafloor cooling at the Eocene-Oligocene onset of the ACC, a past higher geothermal gradient, and removal of overburden.
steps.quote: One possible explanation for the cessation of upward movement of the TZA/CT in the F/MB is a rapid temperature drop at the seafloor

steps.action: The authors reject seafloor cooling: a benthic-foraminiferal cooling of about 10 °C still gives only 32.3 °C at the reflector, below 35 °C.
steps.quote: it cannot account for the thermal conditions required for the Opal-A/CT conversion in the F/MB

steps.action: The authors disfavour a higher palaeo-gradient because the present gradient at DSDP 511 is already higher than in neighbouring areas.
steps.quote: is already higher than those reported in neighboring areas

steps.action: The authors estimate that at 45 °C/km at least about 270 m of eroded overburden would have brought the front to the 35 °C threshold.
steps.quote: an excess of ca. 270 m overburden would account for the minimum thermal requirement for Opal-A/CT conversion

steps.action: The authors support overburden removal with published evidence: anomalous organic maturation at DSDP 511 (Dick et al. 1983) and 150–200 m of erosion inferred near DSDP 330 (Ciesielski and Wise 1977).
steps.quote: [...] supported by analysis of the organic carbon content in sediments of Jurassic to Recent age at DSDP Site 511

steps.action: The authors hypothesize that the ACC and intensified deep and bottom water masses after Antarctic glaciation scoured at least 270 m of sediment in an Early-Middle Miocene erosional phase, fossilizing the fronts.
steps.quote: We thus hypothesize that the large-scale reorganization of oceanic circulation following the opening of the Southern Ocean gateways

steps.action: The authors keep the claim that both reflectors are fossilized Opal-A/CT fronts arrested by erosion-driven cooling; the erosion mechanism remains a hypothesis.
steps.quote: supports their interpretation as fossilized or arrested silica diagenetic fronts

tree.answer: Two cross-cutting reflectors (a BSR and an NBSR) on the new seismic data
No; the reflectors are imaged, but their origin and state are inferred from seismic attributes and drill lithology
Explain the origin of the reflectors (silica diagenesis or gas hydrate) and whether they are active or fossil
Silica diagenesis vs gas hydrate; active vs fossilized; seafloor cooling vs higher palaeo-gradient vs overburden removal
Yes: polarity, frequency and absorption distinguish gas hydrate from silica; temperature at depth distinguishes active from fossil
Conditions found in past traces (seismic and drill cores), not set
Limited: an independent attribute check, a lateral velocity check and a bottom-temperature cross-check; no sensitivity analysis of the temperature calculation
Gas hydrate excluded; fossilized silica fronts kept as the best explanation; Miocene erosion of at least 270 m hypothesized

end.claim: Reflectors XR-F/MB and XR-F/MT are fossilized Opal-A/CT silica diagenetic fronts, arrested by cooling after erosion of at least 270 m of overburden, plausibly by Early-Middle Miocene intensified deep and bottom water masses.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing the computed present temperature at XR-F/MB (22.3 °C) with the 35 °C minimum for Opal-A/CT conversion is what makes the bottom-simulating XR-F/MB a fossil front and motivates the overburden-removal estimate; without it, only the NBSR geometry of XR-F/MT would support fossilization.

gates.evidence: The seismic data come from cruise MSM81, which targeted water-mass exchange (Uenzelmann-Neben 2019), not a hypothesis about diagenetic fronts. The gas-hydrate rival faced a polarity test that could have failed (p. 6). The fossilization claim rests on criteria and a single temperature estimate built from averaged inputs. The erosion mechanism is stated only as a hypothesis (p. 10). Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

Clathrate (gas hydrate) stability under pressure and temperature conditions

limits: Process: the XML text holds only the abstract and the captions, so body steps are located by printed page. The acknowledgments name two reviewers and an associate editor, but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. Uncertainty: the temperature estimate averages three very different gradients (23.9, 38.5 and 74 °C/km) to 45 °C/km and carries no uncertainty or sensitivity analysis; the 270 m figure is a minimum with no stated error. Inference: using DSDP 511's 74 °C/km alone would place XR-F/MB above 35 °C, which the paper does not discuss. Sampling: no core samples the reflectors, so Opal-CT presence at the reflector depth is not observed directly. Sub-claim statuses: gas-hydrate origin excluded (could be read as confirmed against that rival, within the polarity test); fossilized state, best_explanation; timing of fossilization by geometric correspondence, best_explanation; minimum 270 m erosion, estimate without stated resolution; erosion by Miocene bottom water, hypothesis only (claim_status none). Text: the paper refers to 'Section 3.3' and 'Section 6.1/6.2', which do not exist in the published structure, and has typos ('fron', 'SR-F/MB').
